c.tagline: The 'City of the Sun': dunes, buggy rides and Ponta Negra beach.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered; ride-hailing apps like Uber and 99 are usually cheaper than street taxis.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the military police, 192 summons a SAMU ambulance, and 193 reaches the fire brigade.

hood_landmark.Ponta Negra: Ponta Negra Beach and Morro do Careca, Natal

avoid.reason: Caution away from main tourist beaches; some peripheral areas high-crime

hood_desc: Natal's main tourist neighborhood and beach, backed by the iconic Morro do Careca dune and packed with hotels, pousadas, beachfront bars, restaurants and nightlife; the default base for visitors.
A hotel corridor of large beachfront resorts running along the coastal dunes between the city and Ponta Negra, fronted by quiet protected beach; suits travelers wanting all-inclusive resort comfort.

An older beachside district near the center around Praia dos Artistas and Areia Preta, with a nostalgic local seaside feel, seafood spots and the nearby Fort of the Three Wise Men; a lower-key beach base.
One of Natal's leafy upscale residential districts inland from the coast, with tree-lined streets, restaurants, shopping and business hotels; calm and convenient for those not fixated on the beach.
The city's historic riverside port quarter with early-20th-century architecture, theaters and a slowly reviving cultural and nightlife scene; more sightseeing and character than beach.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am to midnight; there is no metro, so late-night travel relies on taxis and ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Natal has no metro or urban rail — the city runs on a municipal and metropolitan bus network (managed by the STTU), with taxis and ride-hailing apps filling the gaps to the Ponta Negra hotel zone and the Via Costeira.
transit.pay: Pay cash to the driver or tap a rechargeable transit card on buses; a single bus fare is about R$4.50.

tip.r: A 10% service charge is usually already added to restaurant bills; extra tipping is optional.

food.name: Carne de Sol
food.desc: Beef lightly salted and sun-dried in the sertao, grilled and served with macaxeira, butter cheese and farofa. The signature dish of Rio Grande do Norte.

places.name: Mangai
places.note: Vast northeastern buffet of wood-fired regional cooking; the reference point for carne de sol in Natal.

places.name: Farofa D'Agua
places.note: Refined potiguar kitchen whose carne de sol with its house farofa is the most ordered plate.

places.name: Camaroes Potiguar
places.note: Family-friendly local classic that does the meat dishes as well as the shrimp.

food.name: Ginga com Tapioca
food.desc: Natal's own street snack: tiny fried ginga fish folded inside a hot tapioca crepe, eaten by hand at the fishing beaches.

places.name: Bar Sandra e Ivanize
places.note: Box 3 at the Redinha market, the traditional address for ginga com tapioca.

places.name: Mercado da Redinha
places.note: The whole market is lined with ginga stalls; go late morning while the fish is fresh.

places.name: Casa de Taipa
places.note: Best-known tapioca house in town, with ginga and carne de sol fillings in a tourist-friendly setting.

food.name: Camarao
food.desc: Potiguar shrimp in every possible form: grilled, in coconut milk, breaded, in pumpkin, or with cheese. Rio Grande do Norte is Brazil's shrimp state.

places.name: Camaroes Potiguar
places.note: The shrimp institution of Natal, with a menu built almost entirely around it.

places.name: NAU Frutos do Mar
places.note: Upmarket seafood house with more than forty shrimp preparations plus fish and shellfish.

places.name: Manary Gastronomia e Arte
places.note: Smart beachfront dining room for a special dinner facing Ponta Negra beach.

food.name: Peixada and Crab
food.desc: Peixada potiguar of white fish stewed with coconut milk, peppers and coriander, plus whole crabs cracked open at beachfront tables.

places.name: Barraca do Caranguejo
places.note: Long-running crab shack on the beach strip, loud, casual and very local.

places.name: NAU Frutos do Mar
places.note: Careful, modern versions of the coastal fish stews and shellfish plates.

places.name: Old Five
places.note: Right on the sand at Ponta Negra with sea views and a seafood-heavy menu.

food.name: Tapioca and Cuscuz Breakfast
food.desc: Cassava-starch tapioca crepes and steamed corn cuscuz with butter, cheese or dried meat. The standard northeastern breakfast.

places.name: Casa de Taipa
places.note: Sweet and savoury tapiocas all day, including carne de sol with nata.

places.name: Mangai
places.note: Enormous regional breakfast spread of cuscuz, tapioca, cakes and tropical fruit.

places.name: Mercado da Redinha
places.note: Market stalls making tapioca to order beside the fish counters.

food.name: Cartola and Northeastern Sweets
food.desc: Fried banana layered with butter cheese, sugar and cinnamon, plus cocada, doce de leite and cakes made with tapioca and corn.

places.name: Mangai
places.note: Dessert table of regional sweets and cakes that is worth the visit on its own.

places.name: Farofa D'Agua
places.note: Traditional potiguar desserts given a modern restaurant treatment.

places.name: Casa de Taipa
places.note: Sweet tapiocas with banana, cheese, coconut and doce de leite.

food.name: Tropical Fruit Juices
food.desc: Cashew fruit, caja, umbu, seriguela, acerola and graviola blended fresh. The northeast has fruits found almost nowhere else in Brazil.

places.name: Mangai
places.note: Long list of regional juices poured alongside the buffet, a good crash course.

places.name: Mercado da Redinha
places.note: Juice stalls pressing whatever fruit came in that morning, at market prices.

places.name: Casa de Taipa
places.note: Fresh juices and batidas to go with the tapiocas.

food.name: Caipirinha and Cold Beer
food.desc: Cachaca caipirinhas made with local cashew or caja fruit, and very cold beer drunk in small glasses at the beach barracas.

places.name: Barraca do Caranguejo
places.note: Classic beach bar for cold beer and crab with your feet almost in the sand.

places.name: Old Five
places.note: Sea-view bar and restaurant on the Ponta Negra beachfront, busy at sunset.

places.name: Camaroes Potiguar
places.note: Fruit caipirinhas designed to go with the shrimp menu.

landmarks: Forte dos Reis Magos
A five-pointed Portuguese fortress from 1598 juts into the sea at the Potengi rivermouth, marking the very spot where Natal was born.
Morro do Careca (Ponta Negra Beach)
A colossal 120-meter sand dune plunging into the ocean crowns Natal's liveliest beach, the city's undisputed postcard image.
Genipabu Dunes and Lagoon
Just north of the city, buggy rides careen over shifting golden dunes to freshwater lagoons and even dromedary camel rides.
Cajueiro de Pirangi (World's Largest Cashew Tree)
A single cashew tree sprawling across two acres near Pirangi beach holds the Guinness record and shades an entire village square.
Parque das Dunas
South America's largest urban park on dunes, a protected Atlantic-forest wilderness with trails, exhibitions and abundant wildlife beside the beach avenue.
Ponte Newton Navarro
An elegant cable-stayed bridge soaring over the Potengi River, best photographed at sunset from Redinha beach or the fortress ramparts.
Centro de Turismo de Natal
A hilltop former prison reborn as a handicrafts market, its cells now stalls of lace and cashews, with sweeping river views.
Catedral Metropolitana de Natal
The strikingly modernist concrete cathedral on Praça da Sé, whose sail-like silhouette and luminous interior surprise visitors expecting colonial architecture.
Igreja de Santo Antônio (Igreja do Galo)
An eighteenth-century baroque church in the old Cidade Alta, nicknamed for its rooftop bronze rooster and housing a small sacred-art museum.
Maracajaú Reefs (Parrachos de Maracajaú)
An hour north, catamarans sail to turquoise natural pools atop coral reefs, the 'Brazilian Caribbean' for snorkeling day trips.

train.note: No intercity passenger trains. Natal has a small CBTU suburban rail line to Parnamirim and Ceará-Mirim, useful locally but not for travel between cities. Everything else is by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária Nova on the southern edge of town has Expresso Guanabara and Nordeste services to Fortaleza (about 8 hours), João Pessoa (3), Recife (4) and Salvador; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/). Buggy transfers rather than buses are the usual way to reach the dune beaches at Genipabu and Pipa.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry. The Potengi river has a small boat crossing to Redinha used by locals, and catamaran trips run up the river and along the coast as excursions. Natal's port handles cargo and cruise ships.

half.name: Pipa
half.blurb: A beach town south of Natal known for cliffside dunes, sea turtles, and the Baía dos Golfinhos dolphin bay.

half.name: São Miguel do Gostoso
half.blurb: A former fishing village turned kitesurfing destination, with steady trade winds and quieter beaches than Natal's coast.
